description: Illustrative cross-framework mappings written for the demo. They are reviewable assertions, NOT official equivalence. All are imported with reviewStatus 'unreviewed' and isIllustrative true; a qualified reviewer must approve or reject each before relying on it.
author: SentinelGRC AI project (not NIST, ISO, AICPA or the EU)

mappings.rationale: Both address defining and enforcing access permissions; ISO A.5.15 also covers access-control rules beyond least privilege.
Privileged access rights are a subset of the permissions PR.AA-05 expects to be managed and reviewed.
Role-based access and modification of access overlaps with managing and reviewing permissions.
Supplier risk is understood and managed in both; ISO frames it as supplier-relationship security.
Vendor and business partner risk management covers assessing and monitoring third-party risk.
Network monitoring for adverse events is one part of ISO monitoring activities.
Monitoring system components for anomalies relates to network monitoring.
Using threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact to understand risk aligns with the ISMS risk assessment process.
Executing the incident response plan corresponds to responding to information security incidents.
Responding to identified security incidents through a defined program.
Both require backups to be created, protected and tested.
Backup and recovery infrastructure supports availability commitments.
Maintaining and replacing software commensurate with risk relates to managing technical vulnerabilities.
Cryptography is one possible security-of-processing measure; Art. 32 compliance needs separate legal and risk-based evidence.
Incident management planning supports breach notification readiness, but the 72-hour notification duty needs its own evidence.
Supplier agreements are where processor obligations are typically contracted.
Both address third-party AI risks; ISO 42001 frames them as third-party and customer relationships.
Characterizing impacts on individuals and society aligns with assessing impacts of AI systems.
Bias evaluation informs data governance, but Art. 10 obligations apply only to high-risk systems and require legal applicability review.
Incident communication processes support, but do not by themselves satisfy, serious-incident reporting duties.
Defining human-AI configurations and oversight responsibilities relates to the human-oversight requirement.
